name: Business Analysis Foundations
lens: What business analysts do and how they create value
summary: Start from zero: what business analysis is, the roles an analyst plays, the six core concepts that every analysis uses, how work moves from need to solution, and what good analysts deliver.

project.title: Business analysis in a real organization
project.brief: Pick an organization you know (a bank branch, a hospital clinic, a campus service). Describe one problem it has, who is affected, what change could help, and what an analyst would need to find out before recommending anything. One page.

lessons: What is business analysis? Problems, needs and solutions
Business analyst roles and titles across industries
The six core concepts of business analysis
The BABOK Guide knowledge areas at a glance
From business need to delivered solution: the analyst's path
Business analyst versus product, project and data roles
Typical business analysis deliverables and who reads them
Skills of a strong business analyst
notes: Be method-neutral and teach BABOK Guide v3 concepts accurately in your own words (six knowledge areas, the Business Analysis Core Concept Model). Hedge anything about exam details; say 'check the IIBA site for the current guide'. Use everyday organizations (bank, clinic, retailer, university) for examples; label invented numbers illustrative.

name: Business Needs, Strategy and Business Cases
lens: Find the real problem and justify the change
summary: Analyze the current state, define the future state and the gap between them, find root causes, size options and write a business case a sponsor can approve.

project.title: A one-page business case
project.brief: Choose a realistic improvement (for example, replacing a manual approval step). Write a one-page business case: problem, current and future state, two options, costs and benefits with simple numbers, risks and your recommendation.

lessons: Business needs: symptoms, problems and opportunities
Analyzing the current state
Defining the future state and the gap
Root cause analysis: 5 Whys and fishbone diagrams
SWOT, PESTLE and other strategic frames, used lightly
Defining solution options and scope
Costs, benefits, payback and return: the numbers in a business case
Writing and presenting a business case
notes: Every financial calculation (payback, ROI, NPV at beginner level, cost-benefit tables) MUST be computed with python and match the text. Show a fishbone as an indented text outline. Include a worked business case with a table of options.

name: Elicitation and Collaboration
lens: Draw out what people really need
summary: Prepare for and run interviews, workshops, surveys, observation and document analysis, confirm what you heard, and keep stakeholders collaborating.

project.title: An elicitation plan and interview guide
project.brief: For a project of your choice, write an elicitation plan (who, which technique, when, why) and a 10-question interview guide for the most important stakeholder, with the follow-up probes you would use.

lessons: Why elicitation is hard: people do not know what they need
Preparing for elicitation: goals, stakeholders and techniques
Interviews: questions that find real needs
Running a requirements workshop
Surveys and questionnaires that give usable answers
Observation and job shadowing
Document analysis, interface analysis and data as sources
Brainstorming, focus groups and prototypes as elicitation
Confirming results and managing stakeholder collaboration
notes: Provide sample interview scripts as short dialogues and sample workshop agendas as tables. Teach open versus closed questions, leading questions, and active listening. No stereotypes about people.

name: Planning and Governing Your Analysis Work
lens: Plan the analysis before you start
summary: Choose an approach, plan stakeholder engagement, decide how requirements will be governed, estimate analysis effort, and measure how well your analysis work is going.

project.title: A business analysis plan
project.brief: Write a one-to-two page business analysis plan for a project of your choice: approach, deliverables, stakeholders and engagement, how requirements will be approved and changed, effort estimate and risks to the analysis.

lessons: Planning business analysis: why analysts need a plan
Choosing a business analysis approach: predictive, agile or hybrid
Stakeholder analysis and engagement planning for analysts
Governance: who decides, approves and signs off requirements
Information management: where requirements live and how they are found
Estimating business analysis effort
Monitoring and improving the analysis work
notes: Include a sample BA plan outline, a stakeholder engagement table and an effort-estimate worked example (verify arithmetic in python). Tool-neutral.

name: Requirements Analysis and Specification
lens: Write requirements that can be built and tested
summary: Classify and write requirements correctly, remove ambiguity, prioritize with MoSCoW and other methods, organize them into a specification and check their quality.

project.title: A requirements specification excerpt
project.brief: Write a requirements specification for one feature of a system you know: business, stakeholder, functional and non-functional requirements (at least 12), each with an ID, a priority and a way to verify it.

lessons: What a requirement is: needs, wants and constraints
Requirement types: business, stakeholder, solution, transition
Functional requirements: writing statements a developer can build
Writing clearly: ambiguity, weak words and testable wording
Requirements quality checklist: complete, consistent, verifiable
Prioritizing requirements: MoSCoW, value versus effort, Kano
Business requirements documents, functional specs and SRS compared
Requirements packages for different audiences
Assumptions, constraints and dependencies
notes: Include many weak-to-strong requirement rewrites as before/after pairs, and a sample requirements table with ID, statement, priority and verification. Do not claim a single standard template; mention IEEE 29148 only as an example, hedged.

name: User Stories, Use Cases and Acceptance Criteria
lens: Capture behavior in stories, scenarios and criteria
summary: Write user stories with the INVEST checklist, split large stories, describe scenarios as use cases, and write acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then form.

project.title: Stories and acceptance criteria for a feature
project.brief: Take a feature (for example, password reset or booking a time slot). Write five user stories, split one that is too big, write Given-When-Then acceptance criteria for two of them and one use case with a main flow and two alternate flows.

lessons: User stories: the card, the conversation and the confirmation
Writing good stories with the INVEST checklist
Splitting large stories without losing value
Epics, themes and the story map
Acceptance criteria: rules and Given-When-Then scenarios
Use cases: actors, goals, main flow and alternate flows
Choosing between stories, use cases and plain requirements
Edge cases, error paths and negative scenarios
notes: Provide worked examples for each technique with realistic features. Show use cases as numbered text. Teach Given-When-Then neutrally (call it Gherkin-style) and do not claim one right format.

name: Non-Functional Requirements and Quality Attributes
lens: Specify how well the system must work
summary: Capture performance, security, usability, reliability, accessibility and compliance requirements in measurable terms and balance them against cost.

project.title: Measurable non-functional requirements
project.brief: For a system of your choice, write eight measurable non-functional requirements covering performance, availability, security, usability, accessibility and data retention, each with a measure and a target.

lessons: What non-functional requirements are and why they get missed
Performance and capacity requirements with real numbers
Availability, reliability and recovery
Security, privacy and compliance requirements
Usability and accessibility requirements
Writing measurable quality attributes and negotiating trade-offs
notes: Availability arithmetic (for example, 99.9% allows about 8.76 hours of downtime a year) and capacity numbers MUST be computed with python. Do not state legal requirements for specific jurisdictions as facts beyond naming well-known regimes (GDPR, WCAG, PCI DSS) at a high level; say 'check current regulations'.

name: Modeling for Analysts
lens: Draw the system so everyone sees the same thing
summary: Use context diagrams, data flow diagrams, entity relationship diagrams and basic UML to show scope, data and behavior, and pick the right diagram for the question.

project.title: A set of models for one system
project.brief: For a small system of your choice (a library loan desk, a clinic booking tool), draw a context diagram, one data flow diagram level, an entity relationship diagram and a UML activity or sequence diagram in text form, and write one paragraph on what each shows.

lessons: Why analysts model: pictures that remove misunderstandings
The context diagram: scope on one page
Data flow diagrams: how data moves
Entity relationship diagrams: the data behind the system
UML essentials: use case, class and activity diagrams
Sequence and state diagrams in plain terms
Choosing the right model for the question
Keeping models consistent with the requirements
notes: Draw all diagrams as ASCII/text in ```text blocks or as indented outlines, never images. Keep notation correct (DFD external entities, processes, data stores, flows; ERD cardinality).

name: Process Modeling and Improvement
lens: See how work flows, then make it flow better
summary: Map processes in BPMN, find waste and bottlenecks, measure cycle time, and design a better to-be process with controls and measures.

project.title: As-is and to-be process
project.brief: Map an everyday process you know (expense approval, returns, onboarding) as-is in text-form BPMN with swimlanes, measure or estimate where time goes, then design a to-be version and explain what changes and what risk the change creates.

lessons: Why processes matter: inputs, steps, outputs and owners
BPMN basics: events, tasks, gateways and flows
Swimlanes and handoffs: who does what
Mapping the as-is process from interviews and data
Measuring a process: cycle time, wait time and rework
Finding waste and bottlenecks: lean thinking for analysts
Designing the to-be process
Controls, exceptions and compliance in processes
Automation, RPA and when not to automate
notes: Show BPMN as structured text (e.g., Lane: Finance; Start event; Task; Exclusive gateway with conditions). Cycle-time, wait-time, throughput and process-efficiency arithmetic MUST be computed with python. Name BPMN 2.0 correctly and accurately.

name: Business Rules, Decision Tables and Data Requirements
lens: Capture the logic and the data precisely
summary: Separate business rules from process, write them clearly, model complex logic as decision tables and decision trees, and define data requirements with a data dictionary.

project.title: Decision table and data dictionary
project.brief: Choose a rule-heavy process (loan pre-qualification, discount eligibility, shipping charges). Write the rules in plain statements, build a decision table that covers every combination, and a data dictionary for the fields involved.

lessons: Business rules: what they are and how they differ from requirements
Writing atomic, testable business rules
Decision tables: every case, no gaps, no overlaps
Decision trees and rule hierarchies
Data requirements and the data dictionary
Data quality rules, reference data and validation
notes: Decision tables must be verified by python enumeration (complete and non-overlapping). Show tables in markdown. Use a realistic eligibility or pricing example.

name: Wireframes and Prototyping for Analysts
lens: Show it before it is built
summary: Sketch screens and flows, use wireframes to elicit and confirm requirements, write annotations developers can use and run a simple usability review.

project.title: A wireframe set with annotations
project.brief: Sketch (on paper or in a free tool, then describe in text) three screens for a feature of your choice with annotations for fields, validations and error messages, and write a five-question usability review script.

lessons: Why prototypes find requirements that talk cannot
Low-fidelity wireframes: sketching screens and flows
Annotating wireframes: fields, rules, validations and messages
Prototypes and mockups: when higher fidelity is worth it
Running a simple usability review with stakeholders
Connecting wireframes to requirements and acceptance criteria
notes: Describe wireframes as text layouts in ```text blocks (boxes and labels in ASCII). Tool-neutral (mention Figma, Balsamiq or pencil and paper only as examples; no pricing or feature claims).

name: Solution Options and Evaluation
lens: Choose the right solution and check that it worked
summary: Compare solution options, assess vendor and build-or-buy decisions, define success measures and evaluate whether the delivered solution creates the expected value.

project.title: A solution comparison and evaluation plan
project.brief: Compare three options for a business need with a weighted scoring table, recommend one, then write how you would judge after launch whether it delivered the value you promised.

lessons: Defining solution options and what 'good enough' means
Build, buy or configure: a decision guide
Weighted scoring and comparing options fairly
Requests for information and proposals from an analyst's point of view
Defining measures of success before delivery
Evaluating a solution after launch
Recommending improvements and retiring what no longer works
notes: All weighted scoring arithmetic MUST be verified in python. Do not quote vendor prices. Include a worked comparison table.

name: Traceability and Managing Change to Requirements
lens: Keep requirements true as everything moves
summary: Trace requirements from need to test, assess the impact of change, baseline and version them, and keep requirements approved, current and retired cleanly.

project.title: A traceability matrix and change request
project.brief: For ten requirements, build a traceability matrix from business objective to requirement to design item to test case, then write one change request and its impact analysis.

lessons: Why requirements change and why that is normal
Traceability: linking need, requirement, design and test
Requirements baselines and versioning
Change requests and impact analysis
Approving, rejecting and prioritizing changes
Requirements status through their life: proposed to retired
Requirements management tools versus spreadsheets
notes: Show a traceability matrix as a markdown table and a change request form as a text block. Count-based checks (coverage percentages) MUST be verified in python.

name: Business Analysis in Agile Teams
lens: Analysis that keeps pace with the sprint
summary: Work as an analyst in Scrum and Kanban teams: groom the backlog, prepare stories, support the product owner, analyze just in time and keep documentation lean but useful.

project.title: A sprint-ready backlog slice
project.brief: Take an epic and prepare a backlog slice for the next two sprints: refined stories with acceptance criteria, a definition of ready, dependencies and the questions that must be answered before sprint planning.

lessons: Where the business analyst fits in an agile team
Backlog refinement: getting stories ready
The definition of ready and the definition of done
Just-in-time analysis and spikes
Working with the product owner and the team
Lean documentation: what to write and what to skip
Analysis in Kanban and continuous delivery
Agile anti-patterns for analysts
notes: Be accurate about Scrum (Scrum Guide roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers; there is no 'business analyst' role in the guide, analysts work within the team). Verify any capacity or story-point arithmetic in python.

name: Business Analysis in Predictive and Hybrid Projects
lens: Analysis in plan-driven delivery
summary: Run requirements work in stage-gated projects: documents, reviews, sign-offs, phase exits and handoffs, and adapt to hybrid delivery.

project.title: A requirements phase plan
project.brief: For a plan-driven project, write the requirements phase plan: activities, documents, reviews, sign-off authority, entry and exit criteria and the plan for late change.

lessons: Predictive delivery: where analysis happens
Requirements documents, reviews and sign-off
Phase gates, entry criteria and exit criteria
Handing requirements to design, build and test
Late change in a plan-driven project
Hybrid delivery: choosing what to plan and what to iterate
notes: Even-handed about methods. Provide a sample phase table and review checklist.

name: Verification, Validation and UAT
lens: Prove the solution matches the requirements and the need
summary: Review requirements, support testing, write UAT scenarios, triage defects and decide whether the solution is ready to go live.

project.title: A UAT plan
project.brief: Write a user acceptance test plan for a feature of your choice: scope, scenarios traced to requirements, entry and exit criteria, defect severity rules and the go-live recommendation criteria.

lessons: Verification and validation: right build versus right thing
Reviewing requirements: walkthroughs and inspections
Test levels and where the analyst contributes
Writing UAT scenarios from acceptance criteria
Running UAT and managing testers
Defect triage and severity versus priority
The go or no-go recommendation
notes: Show a sample UAT scenario table, a defect log and severity/priority matrix. Verify any pass-rate arithmetic in python.

name: Transition, Adoption and Benefits Realization
lens: Make the change stick and prove the value
summary: Plan the transition, training and cutover from the analyst's side, measure adoption, track benefits against the business case and close the loop.

project.title: A transition and benefits plan
project.brief: Write the transition plan for a new system (training, data migration checks, cutover support, adoption measures) and a benefits tracking table comparing the business case promises with how you will measure them.

lessons: Transition requirements: what must be true on day one
Training, documentation and support needs
Data migration requirements and checks
Measuring adoption after go-live
Benefits realization: did the business case hold
Lessons learned and closing the analysis
notes: Include a sample benefits table with baseline, target and actual; verify arithmetic in python. Hedge on change frameworks (name Kotter, ADKAR briefly as examples).

name: SQL for Business Analysts
lens: Query the data to check, reconcile and report
summary: Learn SQL from zero with an analyst's lens: select and filter data, join tables, aggregate, check data quality, reconcile counts and totals, and answer business questions on a real practice dataset.

project.title: Reconciliation and reporting queries
project.brief: Write five SQL queries on the practice data: a count reconciliation between two tables, a missing-data check, a monthly summary, a top-N report and a duplicate check. For each, state the business question and the result you expect.

lessons: Tables, rows, keys and what one row means
SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY: asking your first questions
Filtering with AND, OR, IN, BETWEEN and LIKE
NULL: missing data and why it breaks comparisons
Aggregation: COUNT, SUM, AVG and GROUP BY
HAVING and the order SQL runs a query
JOINs: INNER and LEFT, and what each keeps
Reconciling two sources: counts, totals and mismatches
Data quality checks: duplicates, gaps and impossible values
Dates, CASE and building a clean report query
notes: DATA MODULE: use the TuneBox dataset exactly as described in /home/claude/content-pm2/SCHEMA.md (SQLite at /home/claude/content-pm2/data/tunebox.db). EVERY SQL query MUST be executed and its true output pasted (under 12 lines, under 20 lines of code per block). No SQL comments (--). Analyst lens: reconciliation, validation and reporting, not product experiments. Say 'in the TuneBox practice data'.

name: Excel and Spreadsheet Analysis
lens: Analyze, check and present with a spreadsheet
summary: Use formulas, lookups, pivots, conditional logic and charts to analyze data, and build checks so a spreadsheet can be trusted.

project.title: A checked analysis workbook
project.brief: Build (or fully describe) a workbook with a raw data sheet, a cleaned table, lookup columns, a pivot-style summary and a checks area that proves the totals reconcile. Document each formula in plain language.

lessons: The spreadsheet as an analysis tool: structure and good habits
Formulas, absolute references and common errors
Lookups: VLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, and XLOOKUP
Logical and text functions: IF, AND, OR, SUMIFS, COUNTIFS
Cleaning data in a spreadsheet
Pivot tables: summarizing without formulas
Charts that tell the truth
Checks, reconciliation and protecting a model
Scenario tables and what-if analysis
notes: Show formulas as text with a small data table and the computed result; EVERY result MUST be computed with python (pandas or plain python) and match. Note that function availability varies by version (XLOOKUP is in newer Excel and Google Sheets). Do not rely on screenshots.

name: Data Analysis and Reporting for Analysts
lens: Turn data into a trustworthy answer
summary: Frame a question, profile and clean data, summarize with the right statistics, compare groups carefully and write findings with the right caveats.

project.title: An analysis memo
project.brief: Using the practice data, answer one business question: state the question, describe the data and its limits, show the numbers, give a recommendation and list two caveats. Keep it to one page.

lessons: From business question to analysis plan
Profiling a dataset: size, types, ranges and gaps
Cleaning data: missing values, duplicates and outliers
Summarizing: mean, median, percentiles and spread
Comparing groups and avoiding false conclusions
Correlation is not causation: reading relationships carefully
Writing findings: question, evidence, caveat, recommendation
Reporting cycles: building a report that runs every month
notes: DATA MODULE: use the TuneBox dataset (see SCHEMA.md; SQLite at /home/claude/content-pm2/data/tunebox.db and CSVs). EVERY query/code block and every number MUST be executed and pasted from real output. SQL or Python (pandas) are fine; no SQL comments. Beginner level statistics only. Say 'in the TuneBox practice data'.

name: Dashboards and Visualization for Analysts
lens: Show the numbers so people can act
summary: Choose the right chart, design a clear dashboard, define metrics precisely, avoid misleading visuals and tell a story with data.

project.title: A dashboard specification
project.brief: Write a dashboard specification for a business team: the questions it answers, 6 metrics with exact definitions, the chart for each, filters, refresh frequency and the users who must act on it.

lessons: Visualization basics: matching the chart to the question
Bar, line, scatter and tables: when to use each
Misleading charts and how to spot them
Metric definitions: numerator, denominator and time window
Designing a dashboard people actually use
Data storytelling: the headline, the evidence and the ask
BI tools in practice: Power BI, Tableau, Looker Studio and Excel
notes: DATA MODULE: use the TuneBox dataset (see SCHEMA.md) for every number; EVERY metric you quote MUST be computed from real queries and pasted. Draw charts as ASCII/text tables or bar rows in ```text blocks, never images. Tool-neutral, no feature or price claims; say 'check the current documentation'.

name: Technology Literacy for Analysts
lens: Understand the systems you are analyzing
summary: Understand databases, APIs, integrations, architecture and security basics well enough to ask good questions, write technical requirements and talk to engineers.

project.title: An integration requirements brief
project.brief: For two systems that must exchange data (for example, a web store and an accounting system), write an integration brief: what data moves, in which direction and how often, the failure cases, the security needs and the questions you would ask the engineers.

lessons: How software systems are built: client, server and database
Databases and data models in plain terms
APIs: requests, responses and JSON
Integrations: batch, real-time and file-based
Cloud, environments and release pipelines for analysts
Security and privacy basics every analyst should know
Working with engineers: questions that save time
notes: Show JSON and HTTP examples and VERIFY any JSON parsing/arithmetic with python. Teach concepts, not vendor products. Do not make security guarantees; be accurate about basics (authentication versus authorization, encryption in transit and at rest).

name: Stakeholder Management for Analysts
lens: Work with the people who decide, build and use
summary: Identify and analyze stakeholders, build trust, manage conflicting requests, handle resistance and keep sponsors and teams aligned.

project.title: Stakeholder map and conflict plan
project.brief: Map at least eight stakeholders for a project you know by influence and interest, then write how you would resolve a conflict between two of them over a requirement.

lessons: Who the stakeholders are: users, sponsors, SMEs and others
Stakeholder analysis: influence, interest and attitude
Building trust with subject matter experts
Managing conflicting requirements
Handling resistance and difficult conversations
Managing expectations and saying no well
Keeping sponsors engaged
notes: Include a stakeholder register table, example dialogues and a conflict-resolution worked example. Respectful, no stereotypes.

name: Communication and Facilitation
lens: Be understood and get decisions
summary: Write clearly for business and technical readers, present findings, facilitate workshops and meetings, give and receive feedback and communicate across teams and cultures.

project.title: A findings presentation and email
project.brief: Write a five-slide outline (title and key message per slide) presenting an analysis recommendation to a sponsor, and a short follow-up email that confirms the decisions and next steps.

lessons: Writing for business readers: lead with the answer
Writing for technical readers: precise and complete
Presenting analysis: the headline first
Facilitating workshops and decision meetings
Meeting notes, decisions and follow-up
Giving and receiving feedback
Communicating across teams, time zones and cultures
notes: Provide before/after rewrites, templates as text blocks and sample agendas. Invented respectful examples.

name: Business Analysis Tools
lens: Choose and use the tools of the trade
summary: What requirements, diagramming, backlog and collaboration tools do, how to use them well, and how to set up a clean analysis workspace.

project.title: An analysis workspace setup
project.brief: Describe how you would set up the tools for a project: where requirements, diagrams, decisions and tests live, naming conventions, access rules and how a new teammate finds anything quickly.

lessons: What analyst tools do: capture, model, track and share
Backlog and requirements tools: Jira, Azure DevOps and others
Documentation tools: Confluence, SharePoint and wikis
Diagramming and modeling tools: Visio, Lucidchart, draw.io
Wireframing and prototyping tools
Choosing, rolling out and governing tools
notes: Teach the job each tool does first, then name real tools as examples. No prices or feature lists; say 'check current features'. Use sample requirement and ticket text.

name: AI for Business Analysts
lens: Use AI as an assistant, not an autopilot
summary: Where AI helps an analyst (summaries, drafts, test ideas, data checks), how to prompt well, how to review AI output, and how to protect confidential information.

project.title: An AI-assisted analysis workflow
project.brief: Design a repeatable workflow that uses an AI assistant to turn raw interview notes into a draft requirements list: inputs, prompt, review checklist, what must never be pasted in and how you verify the output.

lessons: What AI can and cannot do for a business analyst
Prompting for analysis work: clear context, task and format
Summarizing interviews, documents and meeting notes
Drafting requirements, stories and test cases with AI
Checking data and logic with AI help
Privacy, confidentiality and company policy
Reviewing AI output: errors, invented facts and bias
notes: Tool-neutral (name ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot or Gemini only as examples; no feature claims). Show example prompts and example outputs that contain a flaw the learner must catch. Stress human review and confidentiality.

name: Business Analysis Certifications and Career Paths
lens: Know the credentials and the road ahead
summary: Understand the main business analysis credentials (IIBA and PMI), what each is for, how to choose, how to study, and how business analysts progress in their careers.

project.title: A certification and career plan
project.brief: Write a one-page plan: your current experience, which credential (if any) fits and why, a 12-week study plan, and the first two roles you would target with the skills you will have.

lessons: Business analyst career paths and levels
The IIBA credentials: ECBA, CCBA, CBAP and others
PMI-PBA and other analysis-related credentials
Choosing whether and when to certify
Studying for an exam: the BABOK Guide, practice questions and habits
Moving from analyst to product, project or data roles
notes: IMPORTANT: say 'check the issuing body for current requirements, fees, exam formats and renewal rules'. Do not state fees, pass rates, question counts or hour thresholds unless you are certain; prefer hedged wording. Describe what each credential is for in general terms.

name: Interview-Ready Business Analyst
lens: Turn what you learned into a job
summary: Build a resume and portfolio, answer behavioral and technical interview questions, handle a requirements case and a process case, and start strong in a new role.

project.title: Interview-ready analyst portfolio
project.brief: Prepare three STAR stories, one real or realistic analysis artifact (requirements excerpt, process map or analysis memo) and a two-minute answer to 'tell me about a requirement that changed late'.

lessons: Business analyst resumes: show impact, not duties
Building a portfolio with real artifacts
Behavioral interviews: STAR stories for analysts
Technical questions: SQL, Excel and process modeling
Case interview: gather requirements from a vague brief
Case interview: improve a broken process
Negotiating an offer and the first 90 days
A 30-day interview preparation plan
notes: Include a worked STAR story, a worked requirements case with the questions to ask, and a worked process case with a verified calculation. Hedge any claim about hiring practices ('often', 'commonly').
